brief: Two classic interview tasks: (a) length of the longest common subsequence of two strings, (b) implement merge sort.
key_idea: LCS: dp[i][j] over prefixes, match extends diagonal; merge sort: split in halves, sort recursively, merge with two pointers.
solution:
1. LCS state dp[i][j] = LCS of a[0..i-1] and b[0..j-1]; dp[0][*]=dp[*][0]=0.
2. If a[i-1]==b[j-1]: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1 else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Answer dp[n][m].
3. Merge sort: msort(l,r): if r-l<=1 return; m=(l+r)/2; msort(l,m); msort(m,r); merge.
4. Merge: two pointers into the halves, take the smaller (use <= to keep it stable), copy leftovers, write back from a temp buffer.
5. Edge cases: empty string gives 0; array of size 0/1 is already sorted.
complexity: LCS O(n*m) time, O(n*m) space (O(m) with rolling rows); merge sort O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Given coin denominations with unlimited supply and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins summing exactly to the target (variant: count the number of ways).
key_idea: Unbounded knapsack: dp[x] = min over coins c of dp[x-c]+1; for number of ways loop coins outside, amounts inside.
solution:
1. dp[0]=0, dp[x]=INF for x>0.
2. For x=1..amount, for each coin c<=x: dp[x]=min(dp[x], dp[x-c]+1) if dp[x-c]!=INF.
3. Answer dp[amount], or -1 if INF.
4. Ways variant: ways[0]=1; for each coin c (outer), for x=c..amount: ways[x]+=ways[x-c] (coins outer => combinations, not permutations); use mod if asked.
5. Edge cases: amount 0 -> 0 coins; unreachable -> -1.
dry_run:
Own example (sample coin list garbled): coins={1,5,10,25}, amount=30.
dp[5]=1, dp[10]=1, dp[25]=1, dp[30]=min(dp[29]+1, dp[25]+1, dp[20]+1, dp[5]+1)=2.
Answer 2 (25+5), matching the sample's '30 -> 2 coins'.

brief: Coins have denominations and per-coin weights (costs); with unlimited coins, form exactly the target amount with minimum total weight.
key_idea: Unbounded knapsack where each coin adds w(c) instead of 1: dp[t] = min(dp[t-c] + w(c)).
solution:
1. dp[0]=0, others INF (use long long).
2. For t=1..T, for each coin i with c[i]<=t and dp[t-c[i]]<INF: dp[t]=min(dp[t], dp[t-c[i]]+w[i]).
3. Answer dp[T] or -1 if unreachable.
4. Edge cases: T=0 -> 0; weights can be large so use long long; zero-value coins should be ignored (infinite loop risk otherwise none here since c>=1).

brief: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of an array.
key_idea: Patience sorting: tails[k] = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1; replace with lower_bound.
solution:
1. Keep vector tails (sorted).
2. For each x: it = lower_bound(tails, x); if it==end push x else *it = x.
3. Answer tails.size().
4. O(n^2) alternative: dp[i]=1+max dp[j] for j<i with a[j]<a[i].
5. Edge cases: empty array -> 0; for non-decreasing use upper_bound instead.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: HackWithInfy 2024 easy problem reported only as 'a variation of 0/1 knapsack'; no actual statement is available.
key_idea: Statement unknown; prepare the standard 0/1 knapsack (dp over capacity, iterate capacity downward).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem; only the base technique can be prepared.
2. Base 0/1 knapsack: dp[w] = best value with capacity w; dp all 0.
3. For each item (wt,val): for w=W down to wt: dp[w]=max(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val) (downward = each item once).
4. Common variations: exact capacity (init -INF except dp[0]=0), count ways (sum instead of max), min items, subset-sum (bool/bitset).
5. Answer dp[W].
dry_run:
Own example (base 0/1 knapsack): items (wt,val)=(1,1),(3,4),(4,5); W=7.
After (1,1): dp[1..7]=1. After (3,4): dp[3..]=4, dp[4..]=5. After (4,5): dp[7]=max(5, dp[3]+5=9)=9.
Answer 9.

brief: A variation of LIS asked in the SP basic DSA round; the variation itself is not recorded.
key_idea: Statement unknown; master LIS O(n^2) (flexible for custom pair conditions) and O(n log n) (lower/upper_bound).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual variation.
2. Prepare O(n^2) LIS: dp[i]=1+max dp[j] over j<i with cond(a[j],a[i]); handles any pairwise condition (bitwise, divisibility, difference).
3. Prepare O(n log n): tails array with lower_bound (strict) / upper_bound (non-decreasing).
4. Common twists: print the sequence (store parent), count LIS (cnt array), longest bitonic (LIS from both sides), string version (compare chars).
complexity: Base: O(n^2) or O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example (base O(n^2) LIS): [3,1,2,4].
dp=[1,1,2,3] (4 extends 1,2).
Answer 3.

brief: Decide whether an array can be split into two subsets with equal sum (the reported extra twists were not recalled).
key_idea: Equal partition iff total is even and a subset sums to total/2 (subset-sum bitset).
solution:
1. S = sum; if S is odd -> false.
2. Subset-sum: bitset/bool dp with dp[0]=1; for each x: dp |= dp << x (or loop s downward: dp[s] |= dp[s-x]).
3. Answer dp[S/2].
4. Twist-ready: min difference = min |S-2s| over reachable s; equal size too -> add count dimension dp[cnt][sum].
5. Edge cases: empty array -> true (both empty); negatives need offset (not typical).
complexity: O(n * S) time (O(n*S/64) with bitset), O(S) space

brief: Compute the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings.
key_idea: dp[i][j] = LCS of prefixes; equal chars extend diagonal, else take max of dropping one char.
solution:
1. dp[i][j] for prefixes a[0..i-1], b[0..j-1]; base row/col 0.
2. a[i-1]==b[j-1] -> dp[i-1][j-1]+1; else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
3. Answer dp[n][m]; to print the LCS backtrack from (n,m).
4. Space optimise with two rows if needed.
5. Edge cases: empty string -> 0.
complexity: O(n*m) time, O(m) space with rolling rows
dry_run:
Own example: a="AGGTAB", b="GXTXAYB".
Matches G,T,A,B along the table; dp[6][7]=4.
Answer 4 ("GTAB").

brief: A problem 'based on 0-1 knapsack'; the exact variant is not given.
key_idea: Statement unknown; prepare 0/1 knapsack and its standard twists (exact fill, count ways, min count, 2D capacity).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. Base: dp[w]=max value with capacity w; per item loop w from W down to wt: dp[w]=max(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val).
3. Exact-capacity variant: init dp=-INF except dp[0]=0.
4. Count subsets with sum S: dp[s]+=dp[s-x] (downward).
5. Two capacities (weight and volume): dp[w][v] both loops downward.
dry_run:
Own example (base): items (2,3),(3,4),(4,5),(5,6); W=5.
Best is items 1+2: weight 5, value 7.
dp[5]=7.

brief: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into a sequence of dictionary words.
key_idea: dp[i] = prefix of length i is segmentable; dp[i] = OR over words w ending at i with dp[i-|w|].
solution:
1. Put words in an unordered_set; record max word length L.
2. dp[0]=true.
3. For i=1..n, for len=1..min(i,L): if dp[i-len] and s.substr(i-len,len) in set -> dp[i]=true, break.
4. Answer dp[n].
5. Edge cases: empty string -> true; words may be reused.
complexity: O(n * L * L) time (substring hashing), O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample-style: s="leetcode", dict={leet, code}.
dp[0]=T; dp[4]: "leet" & dp[0] -> T; dp[8]: "code" & dp[4] -> T.
Answer true.

brief: Decide whether a string can be split into a sequence of dictionary words (words reusable).
key_idea: dp[i] true if some dictionary word ends at i and dp[i-len] is true.
solution:
1. Load dictionary into unordered_set, track max word length L.
2. dp[0]=true.
3. For each end i, try lengths 1..L: dp[i] |= dp[i-len] && set has s[i-len..i).
4. Answer dp[n].
5. Edge cases: empty string true; a word longer than s never matches.
dry_run:
Sample: s="leetcode", dict={leet, code}.
dp[4]=T via "leet"; dp[5..7]=F; dp[8]=T via "code" from dp[4].
Answer true (matches sample).

brief: Count arrays of length K with elements in [1,N] where every element is divisible by the previous one; print the count modulo 10000.
key_idea: dp[len][v] = number of chains of length len ending at v; extend each v to all its multiples (harmonic sum).
solution:
1. dp[v]=1 for all v (length 1).
2. Repeat K-1 times: nd[m] += dp[v] for every multiple m of v (m=v,2v,...<=N).
3. Answer = sum dp[v] mod 10000.
4. Inner loop is N/1+N/2+...=O(N log N) per length.
5. Edge cases: K=1 -> N; take mod at every addition.
complexity: O(K * N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run:
Sample N=3, K=2: dp=[1,1,1].
v=1 -> multiples 1,2,3 get +1; v=2 -> 2 gets +1; v=3 -> 3 gets +1.
nd=[1,2,2], sum=5 (matches N=3,K=2 -> 5). For N=2,K=2: nd=[1,2], sum=3 (matches).

brief: Only the title 'Minimum cost for tickets' is known; most likely LeetCode 983: given travel days and prices of 1-day, 7-day and 30-day passes, find the minimum cost to cover all travel days.
key_idea: dp[d] = min cost to cover travel days up to day d; on a travel day take min of buying a 1/7/30-day pass ending today.
solution:
1. Mark travel days in a boolean array up to the last day D.
2. dp[0]=0; for d=1..D: if d not a travel day dp[d]=dp[d-1].
3. Else dp[d]=min(dp[d-1]+c1, dp[max(0,d-7)]+c7, dp[max(0,d-30)]+c30).
4. Answer dp[D].
5. Assumption: the exam statement matches LC 983 (title only given); adjust durations if different.
complexity: O(D) time, O(D) space (D = last travel day, <= 365)

brief: Interview DP question described only as 'a variation of Longest Common Subsequence'; exact variation unknown.
key_idea: Statement unknown; prepare LCS and its common derivatives (print LCS, shortest common supersequence, min deletions, longest common substring, LPS).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual variation.
2. Base: dp[i][j] = a[i-1]==b[j-1] ? dp[i-1][j-1]+1 : max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
3. Derivatives: SCS length = n+m-LCS; min insert+delete = n+m-2*LCS; LPS = LCS(s, reverse(s)).
4. Longest common substring: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1 on match else 0; track max.
5. Print LCS: backtrack from (n,m) following the choice made.
dry_run:
Own example (base LCS): a="abc", b="ac".
dp row a=[1,1], row b=[1,1], row c=[1,2].
LCS=2; SCS length=3+2-2=3 ("abc").

brief: Positions 1..n on a number line; start at x, make exactly k jumps each of length at most z, staying inside [1,n]; count the distinct paths.
key_idea: ways[j][p] = sum of ways[j-1][q] for |p-q|<=z (q!=p if zero-length jumps forbidden), computed with prefix sums.
solution:
1. ways[0][x]=1.
2. For each jump j: build prefix sums of ways[j-1]; ways[j][p] = pre[min(n,p+z)] - pre[max(1,p-z)-1], minus ways[j-1][p] if a jump of length 0 is not allowed.
3. Answer sum of ways[k][p].
4. WARNING: the given sample (n=5,z=1,k=3,x=2 -> 3) does not match path counting: with jumps of length exactly 1 there are 6 paths, while 3 equals the number of distinct reachable end positions {1,3,5}. Clarify what is counted before coding.
5. If the question asks for distinct end positions, just track reachability (bool) instead of counts.
complexity: O(n*k) time with prefix sums, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample n=5,z=1,k=3,x=2 (length-1 jumps only):
after 1 jump: pos1=1,pos3=1; after 2: pos2=2,pos4=1; after 3: pos1=2,pos3=3,pos5=1.
Paths=6, distinct ends=3 -> the stated answer 3 matches distinct ends, so statement is ambiguous.

brief: Find the maximum sum of a non-empty subarray when you may delete at most one element from it (the result must stay non-empty).
key_idea: Two Kadane states: keep[i] = best subarray ending at i with no deletion, del[i] = best ending at i with one deletion used.
solution:
1. keep = a[0], del = -INF, ans = a[0].
2. For i>=1: del = max(del + a[i], keep) (delete a[i] itself -> previous keep, or deletion earlier); keep = max(keep + a[i], a[i]).
3. Compute new del with the OLD keep; ans = max(ans, keep, del).
4. Edge cases: all negative -> answer is the max element (cannot delete to empty); n=1 -> a[0].
dry_run:
Own example: [1,-2,0,3].
i0: keep=1, del=-inf, ans=1.
i1: del=max(-inf,1)=1, keep=max(-1,-2)=-1, ans=1.
i2: del=max(1,-1)=1, keep=0. i3: del=max(4,0)=4, keep=3 -> ans=4.

brief: Given n and k, count arrays of length k with values from 1..n where each element is divisible by the previous one, modulo the given modulus (10000).
key_idea: dp over length with last value; push counts from v to all multiples of v.
solution:
1. dp[v]=1 for v=1..n (length 1).
2. For len=2..k: nd[m] += dp[v] for m in {v,2v,3v,...<=n}.
3. Answer sum of dp mod 10000.
4. Pull formulation is equivalent: dp[len][v] = sum over divisors d of v of dp[len-1][d].
5. Edge cases: k=1 -> n mod 10000.
complexity: O(k * n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Count the ways n people (n even) seated around a table can all shake hands in pairs simultaneously with no two handshakes crossing (statement inferred: Catalan-style).
key_idea: Person 1 shakes with person 2j+2, splitting the rest into two independent even groups: dp[m] = sum dp[j]*dp[m-1-j] (Catalan).
solution:
1. Let m = n/2 pairs; dp[0]=1.
2. dp[m] = sum_{j=0}^{m-1} dp[j]*dp[m-1-j] (person 1's partner leaves j pairs on one side, m-1-j on the other).
3. Answer dp[n/2]; if n is odd answer 0.
4. Use mod 1e9+7 if required (Catalan grows fast).
5. Assumption: the 'number of handshakes' question is the non-crossing variant; if it is simply 'every pair shakes once' the answer is n*(n-1)/2.
dry_run:
Own example: n=6 -> m=3.
dp[1]=1, dp[2]=dp0*dp1+dp1*dp0=2, dp[3]=dp0*dp2+dp1*dp1+dp2*dp0=2+1+2=5.
Answer 5.

brief: Find the minimum number of characters to insert anywhere in a string to make it a palindrome.
key_idea: Answer = n - LPS(s), where LPS = LCS(s, reverse(s)); or interval dp[i][j].
solution:
1. Interval DP: dp[i][j] = min insertions for s[i..j]; dp[i][i]=0.
2. If s[i]==s[j]: dp[i][j]=dp[i+1][j-1]; else 1+min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
3. Iterate i from n-1 down to 0, j from i+1 up.
4. Equivalent: n - LCS(s, rev(s)).
5. Edge cases: empty or single char -> 0.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space (O(n) with LCS rolling rows)
dry_run:
Own example: s="mbadm".
LPS = "mam" (or "mdm"), length 3.
Answer 5-3=2 ("mbdadbm").

brief: A variation of longest non-decreasing subsequence asked in a 45-minute interview round; the variation is not recorded.
key_idea: Statement unknown; base LNDS = patience sorting with upper_bound (equal values allowed to extend).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual variation.
2. Base LNDS: tails array; for each x, it=upper_bound(tails,x); replace or push.
3. O(n^2) form for custom conditions: dp[i]=1+max dp[j] (j<i, a[j]<=a[i], extra condition).
4. Common twists: min removals to make array sorted = n - LNDS; min ops to make k-increasing (LNDS per residue class); LNDS with difference constraints (map of best per value).
complexity: Base: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Count binary strings of length N with no two consecutive 1s such that (#0s - #1s) is a multiple of 3 (return 0 if none).
key_idea: State = (last bit, (#0-#1) mod 3); append 0 always, append 1 only after 0.
solution:
1. dp[b][m] = count of valid prefixes ending with bit b and difference mod 3 = m.
2. Init length 1: dp[0][1]=1 ("0"), dp[1][2]=1 ("1", diff -1 = 2 mod 3).
3. Transition: append 0 from any state -> m+1; append 1 only from b=0 -> m-1 (i.e. m+2).
4. Answer dp[0][0]+dp[1][0] (mod 1e9+7 assumed if large).
5. Edge cases: N=1 -> 0; N=0 -> 1 (empty string) if allowed.

brief: Count strings of length n over vowels using allowed transitions a->e, e->a/i, i->a/e/o/u, o->i/u, u->a, where consecutive moves must alternate between going up and going down alphabetically; answer mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: State = (last vowel, direction of last move); next move must go the opposite direction along an allowed edge.
solution:
1. Index a,e,i,o,u = 0..4; edge u->v is 'up' if v>u else 'down'.
2. Length 1: 5 strings (no direction yet). Length 2: every allowed edge, state (v, dir).
3. For length>=3: from (u, up) take only down edges; from (u, down) only up edges.
4. Answer = sum over states, mod 1e9+7.
5. Edge cases: n=1 -> 5.
dry_run:
Sample: n=1 -> 5; n=2 -> number of edges = 1+2+4+2+1 = 10.
n=3: up-ending states (e1,i1,o1,u2) each take a down edge -> 1+2+1+2=6; down-ending (a3,e1,i1) take up edges -> 3+1+2=6.
Total 12 (matches).

brief: Pick a subsequence of nums with sum exactly target; after picking index i the next pick must be at index >= i + (nums[i] % 4) + 1. Maximise the number of picked elements, or -1.
key_idea: dp[i][t] = max picks using indices >= i with remaining sum t; skip i, or take i and jump to i+gap.
solution:
1. dp[i][t] for i=n..0 (suffix), t=0..target; dp[i][0]=0 for all i; dp[n][t>0]=-INF.
2. Skip: dp[i][t]=dp[i+1][t].
3. Take (if nums[i]<=t): j=i+nums[i]%4+1 (clamp to n); dp[i][t]=max(..., 1+dp[j][t-nums[i]]) if reachable.
4. Answer dp[0][target], -1 if -INF.
5. Assumption: 'next selectable index' means the earliest allowed index (cooldown), later indices also allowed.
dry_run:
Sample nums=[2,3,4,5], target=7.
Take 2 (i=0): gap=2%4+1=3 -> next index >=3 -> take 5 -> sum 7, length 2.
Take 3 (i=1): next >=1+3+1=5 -> nothing. Take 4 then nothing sums to 3.
Answer 2 (matches).

brief: Cover a fence of exact length N using unlimited panels of length a (cost p) and length b (cost q), plus at most one custom panel of any length for a flat fee F; minimise total cost.
key_idea: dp[x] = min cost to cover exactly x with a/b panels; answer = min(dp[N], F + min_{x<N} dp[x]) since the custom panel fills the rest.
solution:
1. dp[0]=0, dp[x]=INF; dp[x]=min(dp[x-a]+p, dp[x-b]+q) for x>=a / x>=b.
2. Without custom panel: dp[N].
3. With custom panel covering the remaining N-x (>=1): F + min over x in [0,N-1] of dp[x].
4. Answer = min of both (always finite since F alone covers N).
5. Edge cases: use long long; if the custom panel must have length >= 1 keep x<N as above.

brief: Paint N houses with C colours so adjacent houses differ, minimising cost subject to a budget B (only a one-line summary exists).
key_idea: Statement incomplete; base is Paint House: dp[i][c] = cost[i][c] + min over c'!=c of dp[i-1][c'] using best/second-best.
solution:
1. Statement too vague (role of budget B unknown: feasibility check, count of ways within B, or maximise houses painted).
2. Base: dp[0][c]=cost[0][c]; dp[i][c]=cost[i][c]+ (c==argmin1 ? min2 : min1) of previous row.
3. Min total = min_c dp[n-1][c]; if the question is feasibility, output it if <= B else -1.
4. If it asks to count colourings with cost <= B: dp[i][c][spent] (O(N*C*B) with best-two trick per spent).

brief: Given two strings, find the minimum number of insert/delete/replace operations to convert the first into the second.
key_idea: dp[i][j] = edit distance between prefixes; match -> diagonal, else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).
solution:
1. dp[i][0]=i, dp[0][j]=j.
2. If a[i-1]==b[j-1]: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1].
3. Else dp[i][j]=1+min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)).
4. Answer dp[n][m].
5. Edge cases: one empty string -> length of the other.
complexity: O(n*m) time, O(n*m) space (O(m) with rolling rows)
dry_run:
Own example: "horse" -> "ros".
horse->rorse (replace h), rorse->rose (delete r), rose->ros (delete e).
dp[5][3]=3.

brief: B buckets, bucket i has r_i red and g_i green balls; draw one ball uniformly from each bucket. Find the probability that exactly K reds are drawn (6 decimals).
key_idea: dp[j] = probability of j reds so far; each bucket: dp'[j] = dp[j]*(1-p_i) + dp[j-1]*p_i with p_i = r_i/(r_i+g_i).
solution:
1. dp[0]=1.
2. For each bucket compute p=r/(r+g); update j from current count down to 0: dp[j] = dp[j]*(1-p) + (j? dp[j-1]*p : 0).
3. Answer dp[K] printed with fixed 6 decimals.
4. Edge cases: K > B -> 0.000000; use double.

brief: Reduce N to 1 with the fewest moves, where a move is: subtract 1, halve (if divisible by 2), or reduce to one third (if divisible by 3).
key_idea: N up to 1e9: memoised f(n)=min(n%2+1+f(n/2), n%3+1+f(n/3)) - only subtract 1 to reach the next multiple before dividing.
solution:
1. Base: f(1)=0, f(2)=f(3)=1.
2. f(n) = min(n%2 + 1 + f(n/2), n%3 + 1 + f(n/3)) (n%2 or n%3 subtractions, then one division).
3. Memoise in unordered_map; only O(log^2 N) distinct states are visited.
4. Do NOT use a dp array to 1e9 (memory) or plain BFS (too slow).
5. 'Reduce by two-thirds' is interpreted as n -> n/3 (verified against samples and a brute force for n<=300).

brief: Find the longest strictly increasing subsequence in which every adjacent chosen pair (a,b) satisfies (a & b) * 2 < (a | b).
key_idea: O(n^2) LIS where the extension test also checks the bitwise condition.
solution:
1. dp[i] = longest valid subsequence ending at i, init 1.
2. For j<i: if a[j]<a[i] and (a[j]&a[i])*2 < (a[j]|a[i]) then dp[i]=max(dp[i], dp[j]+1).
3. Answer max dp[i].
4. Use long long so the *2 cannot overflow.
5. Input sample format: first number is n.

brief: Find the fewest characters to insert into a string to make it a palindrome.
key_idea: Answer = n - longest palindromic subsequence; interval dp[i][j] directly.
solution:
1. dp[i][j] = min insertions for s[i..j], dp[i][i]=0.
2. s[i]==s[j] -> dp[i+1][j-1]; else 1+min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
3. Fill i from n-1 down, j from i+1 up; answer dp[0][n-1].
4. Edge cases: already a palindrome -> 0.
dry_run:
Sample s="abcd": no two equal characters, LPS=1.
dp[2][3]=1, dp[1][3]=2, dp[0][3]=3.
Answer 3 (matches: "dcbabcd").

brief: Longest strictly increasing subsequence where each adjacent chosen pair (a,b) satisfies (a AND b)*2 < (a OR b).
key_idea: Quadratic LIS with an extra pairwise bitwise check on each extension.
solution:
1. dp[i]=1 for all i.
2. For each i, for j<i: if a[j]<a[i] && (a[j]&a[i])*2 < (a[j]|a[i]) -> dp[i]=max(dp[i],dp[j]+1).
3. Answer = max dp (0 for empty).
4. Use 64-bit to avoid overflow in *2.
5. Note the condition is not transitive, so the O(n log n) tails trick does not apply.

brief: N guests must each be served at a distinct positive integer time t (one per time unit); guest i's unhappiness is |C_i - t|. Minimise total unhappiness.
key_idea: Sort C; optimal times are increasing with sorted guests, so dp[i][t] = min cost serving first i guests using times <= t.
solution:
1. Sort C ascending; times only need range 1..2N.
2. dp[i][t] = min(dp[i][t-1] (time t unused), dp[i-1][t-1] + |C_i - t| (serve guest i at t)).
3. dp[0][t]=0, dp[i][0]=INF for i>0.
4. Answer dp[N][2N].
5. Exchange argument: crossing assignments never help, hence sorting.
complexity: O(N^2) time, O(N) space with rolling rows (N<=1e3 -> 2e6 ops)

brief: Reduce N (<=1e9) to 1 using the fewest moves: subtract 1, halve if divisible by 2, or divide by 3 if divisible by 3.
key_idea: Memoised recursion: always subtract just enough to reach a multiple of 2 or 3, then divide.
solution:
1. f(1)=0, f(2)=f(3)=1.
2. f(n)=min(n%2+1+f(n/2), n%3+1+f(n/3)).
3. Memoise with unordered_map (few hundred states for 1e9).
4. A plain dp array up to N is too big for 1e9 - avoid.
5. Verified equal to the naive dp for all n<=300.

brief: Lights with intensities are processed left to right; each is activated or skipped, an activated light adds its intensity, and a threshold K restricts the difference with the nearest activated light; maximise total glow (only a partial preview exists).
key_idea: Statement incomplete; likely dp[i] = a[i] + best dp[j] over earlier j with |a[i]-a[j]| <= K (LIS-like with a value window).
solution:
1. Statement too vague (exact threshold rule hidden), so treat as a guess.
2. If the rule is |a[i] - a[last activated]| <= K: dp[i] = a[i] + max(0, max dp[j] for j<i with |a[j]-a[i]|<=K).
3. O(n^2) directly; O(n log n) with a segment tree over compressed values (range max on [a[i]-K, a[i]+K]).
4. Answer max dp[i] (or 0 if nothing activated).
complexity: Guess: O(n^2) or O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example (under the guessed rule): a=[5,1,6,2], K=1.
dp=[5,1,11 (6 after 5),3 (2 after 1)].
Answer 11.

brief: Given a string of digits and a target number, insert the minimum number of '+' signs between digits so the expression equals the target; return -1 if impossible.
key_idea: dp[i][t] = min number of terms to split suffix s[i..] into numbers summing to t; '+' count = terms - 1.
solution:
1. dp[n][0]=0, dp[n][t>0]=INF.
2. For i=n-1..0, for t=0..T: grow val = s[i..j] digit by digit; stop once val>t; dp[i][t]=min(dp[i][t], 1+dp[j+1][t-val]).
3. Answer dp[0][T]-1, or -1 if INF.
4. Leading zeros are allowed (val just stays small); early break keeps the inner loop short.
5. Edge cases: whole string equals target -> 0 pluses.
complexity: O(n * T * min(n, digits(T)+zeros)) time, O(n*T) space

brief: Count arrays of length N with values in [1,M] having exactly K adjacent pairs (X,Y) that are 'perfectly even' (X*Y - X - Y is even), modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: X*Y-X-Y = (X-1)(Y-1)-1 is even iff both X and Y are even, so only parity matters: dp[i][k][parity of last].
solution:
1. E = M/2 even values, O = M - E odd values.
2. dp[1][0][even]=E, dp[1][0][odd]=O.
3. Next even after even: k+1 (multiply by E); even after odd: k (x E); odd after anything: k (x O).
4. Answer dp[N][K][even]+dp[N][K][odd] mod 1e9+7.
5. Edge cases: K > N-1 -> 0; verified by brute force on small N,M.
dry_run:
Own example N=3, M=3, K=1: E=1 (2), O=2.
len1: e(k0)=1, o(k0)=2. len2: e: k1=1 (2,2), k0=2; o: k0=6.
len3 k=1: e from e(k0)... total = 4 (matches brute force: e.g. 2,2,1 / 2,2,3 / 1,2,2 / 3,2,2).

brief: Particles have positive sizes; any two can merge into one of size |x - y|. Find the minimum size obtainable after combining in any order.
key_idea: Final value = |sum(A) - sum(B)| for some split into two groups (Last Stone Weight II); minimise via subset-sum.
solution:
1. Every merge order corresponds to assigning + or - signs; the result is S - 2*s for a subset sum s <= S/2.
2. Subset-sum boolean dp (or bitset) up to S/2.
3. Answer = S - 2*(largest reachable s <= S/2).
4. Max-heap greedy (always smash two largest) is WRONG.
5. Edge case: single particle -> its size.
complexity: O(n * S) time (O(n*S/64) with bitset), O(S) space
dry_run:
Own example [2,7,4,1,8,1], S=23, half=11.
Reachable sums include 11 (2+8+1)? 2+8+1=11 yes.
Answer 23-22=1.

brief: A digit string (2-9) was typed on a multi-tap keypad; count the distinct messages that could produce it, where each run of equal digits splits into letters (keys 7 and 9 have 4 letters, others 3). Answer mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Runs are independent: for a run of length L, ways f(L) = f(L-1)+f(L-2)+f(L-3) (+f(L-4) for keys 7/9); multiply over runs.
solution:
1. Precompute f3 (tribonacci) and f4 (tetranacci) up to max length with f(0)=1.
2. Scan runs of equal digits: length L, digit d.
3. ans *= (d=='7'||d=='9') ? f4[L] : f3[L], mod 1e9+7.
4. Equivalent single-pass dp: dp[i] = sum of dp[i-k] for k=1..maxPress while the last k chars are equal.
5. Edge cases: single digit -> 1.

brief: Split a string into the minimum number of contiguous substrings such that each is a palindrome; output that count.
key_idea: Precompute isPal[i][j]; dp[i] = min pieces for prefix of length i = min over palindromic s[j..i-1] of dp[j]+1.
solution:
1. isPal[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && (j-i<2 || isPal[i+1][j-1]), fill i descending.
2. dp[0]=0; dp[i] = min_{j<i, isPal[j][i-1]} dp[j]+1.
3. Answer dp[n] (number of pieces = cuts + 1; LeetCode 132 asks cuts, subtract 1 there).
4. Edge cases: palindrome string -> 1; empty -> 0.
dry_run:
Own example s="aab".
isPal: "a","a","b","aa".
dp[1]=1, dp[2]=1 ("aa"), dp[3]=dp[2]+1=2.
Answer 2 ("aa"|"b").

brief: Given two arrays, find the maximum number of gates you can take under (unrecorded) conditions linking the two arrays; reportedly solved with a 2D DP similar to LIS.
key_idea: Statement too vague; likely a 2-D chain problem (sort by one array, LIS on the other, like Russian dolls / box stacking).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. Typical pattern: pairs (a[i], b[i]); you can take gate j after i if a[j]>a[i] and b[j]>b[i].
3. Sort by a ascending (ties: b descending to avoid using equal a), then LIS on b with lower_bound.
4. If order is fixed by index instead, use O(n^2) dp[i]=1+max dp[j] (j<i, both conditions).
complexity: Typical: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example (Russian-doll pattern): pairs (5,4),(6,4),(6,7),(2,3).
Sorted: (2,3),(5,4),(6,7),(6,4); LIS on b: 3,4,7 -> 3.
Answer 3 (under the assumed rule).

brief: Length of the LCS of two strings with additional conditions that were not recalled; brute force and plain DP failed hidden tests.
key_idea: Statement unknown; prepare the O(n*m) LCS plus faster special cases (LCS of permutations -> LIS in O(n log n)).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. Base LCS dp[i][j] with rolling rows (O(m) memory) for large inputs.
3. If plain DP TLEs because n,m ~1e5 and one string has distinct symbols (permutation), map positions and run LIS: O(n log n).
4. Other common extras: LCS with at most k mismatches (add k dimension), LCS where chosen chars must be consecutive in one string (substring), LCS with constraint on gaps.
complexity: Base: O(n*m) time, O(m) space; permutation case O(n log n)

brief: Knapsack-based DP with extra (unrecorded) constraints from a live interview coding round.
key_idea: Statement unknown; each extra constraint usually adds one DP dimension (count of items, second capacity, group, adjacency flag).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. Base 0/1: dp[w]=max(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val), w descending.
3. Item count limit k: dp[c][w], loop c descending too.
4. Second resource: dp[w][v]. Groups (pick <=1 per group): copy row per group and try each item.
5. No two adjacent items: dp[i][w][tookPrev] or dp[i][w]=max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-2][w-wt]+val).
complexity: Base: O(n*W) time; each extra dimension multiplies it
dry_run:
Own example (count limit k=1): items (1,5),(1,4),(2,8); W=2.
Without limit best=9 (5+4); with at most 1 item best=8.
Shows how the count dimension changes the answer.

brief: Two grids of the same size; find the minimum path sum from (0,0) to the bottom-right moving right/down, where you may switch between the two grids at cost S.
key_idea: dp[r][c][g] = min cost to stand on cell (r,c) of grid g; arrive from top/left either in the same grid or from the other grid paying S.
solution:
1. dp[0][0][g] = grid[g][0][0] for g=0,1 (start in either grid; if a fixed start grid is required set the other to INF or +S).
2. For each cell, from each predecessor p (up/left) and grid h: dp[r][c][g] = grid[g][r][c] + min(dp[p][g], dp[p][1-g] + S).
3. Answer min(dp[n-1][m-1][0], dp[n-1][m-1][1]).
4. Assumption: moves are right/down and a switch happens while moving (you pay the new grid's cell value); if switching in place is allowed also relax dp[r][c][g] with dp[r][c][1-g]+S-adjusted values.
5. Use long long.

brief: Count the number of (non-empty) common subsequences of two strings, counting by choice of positions.
key_idea: dp[i][j] = number of common subsequence pairs in prefixes; on match add 1 + dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], else inclusion-exclusion.
solution:
1. dp[0][*]=dp[*][0]=0.
2. If a[i-1]==b[j-1]: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].
3. Else dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] - dp[i-1][j-1].
4. Answer dp[n][m]; take mod (add MOD before subtracting).
5. Note: this counts position-pairs; if DISTINCT common subsequence strings are asked, a different (last-occurrence) DP is required - clarify.

brief: OA problem named 'Vanguard', reportedly solved with a 2D knapsack DP; no statement is available.
key_idea: Statement unknown; prepare 2-constraint 0/1 knapsack dp[w][v] (two capacities, or capacity + item count).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. 2D knapsack: dp[a][b] = best value using resource1 <= a and resource2 <= b.
3. For each item (x,y,val): for a from A down to x, b from B down to y: dp[a][b]=max(dp[a][b], dp[a-x][b-y]+val).
4. 'Exactly k items' variant: second dimension is the count.
dry_run:
Own example (base, LeetCode 474 style): items (zeros,ones)=(1,1),(1,0),(0,1); A=1, B=1; value 1 each.
Take (1,0)+(0,1) -> 2 items.
dp[1][1]=2.

brief: Stock-trading-style problem: sell grains for maximum profit given a rotting period r and a curing period c (memoised DP); full rules not recorded.
key_idea: Statement too vague; likely state machine like 'buy/sell with cooldown': state (day, holding?, days held) with rot deadline r and cooldown c.
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the exact problem (meaning of rotting/curing unknown).
2. Plausible model: after buying on day i you must sell within r days (else grain rots); after selling you wait c days before buying again.
3. dp(i, holding, boughtDay): not holding -> max(skip, buy at i); holding -> max(skip if i-boughtDay<r, sell -> jump to i+c+1).
4. Memoise; O(n*r) states.
dry_run:
Own example (under the guessed model): prices=[1,3,2,8], r=2, c=1.
Buy d0 (1), sell by d2: best sell d1 (3) -> +2, cooldown to d3: nothing left to sell -> 2; or buy d2 (2) sell d3 (8) -> +6.
Answer 6.

brief: N candidates in a line must be assigned exactly N/2 to city A and the rest to city B; assignments carry costs and every adjacent pair in the same city adds a penalty; minimise the total.
key_idea: dp[i][a][last] = min cost for first i candidates with a sent to A and the last one in city 'last'.
solution:
1. State: number assigned to A so far (<= N/2) and city of the previous candidate.
2. Transition to A: + costA[i] + (last==A ? P : 0); to B similarly, respecting the N/2 limits.
3. Answer min(dp[N][N/2][A], dp[N][N/2][B]).
4. This statement omits the per-candidate costs; same as Q0264 (use costs from input; if only penalties exist set costs to 0).
5. Edge cases: N odd -> 'the rest' go to B (limit B count to N - N/2).
complexity: O(N^2) time, O(N) space with rolling arrays
dry_run:
Own example (from the sibling problem): costs [[1,100],[1,100],[100,1],[100,1]], P=10.
AABB: 1+1+1+1 + 10 (A,A) + 10 (B,B) = 24; ABAB = 202.
Answer 24.

brief: Count arrays of length K with values in 1..N such that each a[i+1] is divisible by a[i]; answer modulo 10000.
key_idea: dp[v] = chains ending at v; each step push dp[v] to every multiple of v.
solution:
1. dp[v]=1 for v in 1..N.
2. K-1 times: nd[m] += dp[v] for m = v, 2v, ... <= N.
3. Answer sum dp mod 10000.
4. Harmonic loop -> N log N per step.
5. Edge case: K=1 -> N mod 10000.
complexity: O(K * N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run:
Own example N=4, K=2: from 1 -> 4 multiples, 2 -> {2,4}, 3 -> {3}, 4 -> {4}.
Total 4+2+1+1 = 8.
Answer 8.

brief: Count the ways to choose exactly K elements from Arr (repetition allowed, order ignored, i.e. a multiset of indices) whose sum is at most M, modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: Unbounded knapsack with a count dimension: iterate items outside, count and sum ascending so each item can repeat but order is ignored.
solution:
1. dp[k][s] = number of multisets of size k with sum s; dp[0][0]=1.
2. For each item v (outer loop): for k=1..K: for s=v..M: dp[k][s] += dp[k-1][s-v] (ascending k reuses v -> repetition).
3. Answer = sum over s<=M of dp[K][s].
4. If Arr contains duplicate values, decide whether they are distinct choices (index-based, as here) or dedupe first.
5. Mod 1e9+7 at each addition.
complexity: O(N*K*M) time (1.25e8 at limits, fine in C++), O(K*M) space

brief: Choose an order-preserving subsequence where each consecutive pair (y,x) satisfies x = 2y, 3y, y+1, y-1, y/2 or y/3 (exact division); each chosen element scores its number of divisors; maximise the total score.
key_idea: Scan left to right keeping best[value] = best score of a chain ending with that value; x's predecessors are x/2, x/3, x-1, x+1, 2x, 3x.
solution:
1. d(x) = divisor count by trial division up to sqrt(x).
2. For each x in order: prev = max over y in {x-1, x+1, 2x, 3x, x/2 (if even), x/3 (if divisible by 3)} of best[y] (0 if absent).
3. cur = d(x) + prev; best[x] = max(best[x], cur); ans = max(ans, cur).
4. Relations come from x=2y -> y=x/2, x=y/2 -> y=2x, etc.
5. Edge cases: single element -> d(a0); use long long for sums.

brief: Merge arrays A (length m) and B (length n) into one sequence preserving each array's relative order; the cost is the sum of C[x][y] over consecutive elements x,y in the merged array. Minimise the cost.
key_idea: dp[i][j][s] = min cost after taking i from A and j from B, where s says whether the last element came from A or B (so the last value is known).
complexity: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space (can roll to O(n))

brief: Split positive integers (each 1..300) into two groups whose sizes differ by at most 1 and whose sums are as close as possible; print the two sums, smaller first.
key_idea: Subset-sum with a count dimension: reach[c] = bitset of sums achievable with exactly c elements; pick size n/2.
solution:
1. S = total; reach[0] = {0}.
2. For each x: for c from current max down to 1: reach[c] |= reach[c-1] << x.
3. Group size h = n/2 (other group n-h, differ by <=1).
4. Among sums s in reach[h], minimise |S - 2s|; print min(s,S-s) and max.
5. Edge cases: n=1 -> 0 and the element.
complexity: O(n^2 * S / 64) time with bitset, O(n * S) bits space
dry_run:
Sample [87,100,28,67,68,41,67,1]: n=8, S=459, h=4.
Best 4-element sum near 229.5: 229 (e.g. 100+67+41+... checked by DP).
Output 229 230 (matches).

brief: Count arrays of length K with values in [1,N] where each element divides the next; answer mod 10000.
key_idea: dp over length with last value v; next value is any multiple of v.
solution:
1. dp[v]=1 initially.
2. For each further position: nd[kv] += dp[v] for all multiples kv <= N.
3. Answer = sum dp mod 10000.
4. Complexity driven by the harmonic sum N(1+1/2+...+1/N).
5. Edge case: K=1 -> N.
complexity: O(K * N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run:
Sample n=3, k=2: length-1 dp=[1,1,1].
nd[1]=1, nd[2]=1+1=2, nd[3]=1+1=2.
Sum 5 (matches).

brief: Find the longest increasing subsequence whose consecutive differences are also increasing (n<=500); the sample 1 2 3 4 5 -> 5 shows equal differences are allowed (non-decreasing differences).
key_idea: State must remember the last two picks: dp[i][j] = longest chain ending with picks j<i; extend from dp[j][k] when a[j]-a[k] <= a[i]-a[j].
solution:
1. dp[i][j] = 2 for any j<i with a[j]<a[i].
2. dp[i][j] = max(2, 1 + max dp[j][k]) over k<j with a[k]<a[j] and a[j]-a[k] <= a[i]-a[j].
3. Answer max over all dp, or 1 if n=1 (0 if empty).
4. Use '<=' to match the sample (1 2 3 4 5 -> 5); switch to '<' if strictly increasing differences are required.
5. Speed-up if needed: for fixed j sort k by difference and use prefix max -> O(n^2 log n).
complexity: O(n^3) time (~2e7 for n=500), O(n^2) space

brief: A string of '(', ')' and '*'; count the ways to replace each '*' with '(', ')' or the empty string so that the result is a balanced bracket sequence.
key_idea: dp[b] = number of ways so far with current balance b (never negative); '*' branches into b+1, b-1, b.
solution:
1. dp[0]=1.
2. '(' -> shift to b+1; ')' -> b-1 (drop b=0); '*' -> sum of the three moves.
3. Answer dp[0] at the end.
4. Counts replacement choices (different choices giving the same string are counted separately); take mod 1e9+7 if large.
5. Balance never exceeds n, so arrays of size n+2.
dry_run:
Own example "(*)".
After '(': dp[1]=1. After '*': dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1, dp[2]=1.
After ')': dp[0]=dp[1]=1 -> answer 1 (star = empty).

brief: Find the longest increasing subsequence where the differences between adjacent chosen elements are also increasing.
key_idea: Remember the last two chosen indices: dp[i][j] extends dp[j][k] when a[i]-a[j] > a[j]-a[k].
solution:
1. dp[i][j]=2 for j<i, a[j]<a[i].
2. dp[i][j] = 1 + max dp[j][k] over k<j with a[k]<a[j] and a[j]-a[k] < a[i]-a[j].
3. Answer = max dp (1 if n=1).
4. Strict differences used here; Q0244's sample shows some versions allow equal differences (use <=).
5. For n up to a few thousand, sort predecessors by difference and use prefix max.
dry_run:
Own example [1,2,3,4,5] (strict): 1,2,4 has diffs 1,2 -> 3; extending needs diff > 2 -> none.
dp max = 3 (e.g. 1,2,4 or 1,2,5).
Answer 3.

brief: A hard 0/1-knapsack-style DP problem from a 4-question SP OA; only the topic is known.
key_idea: Statement unknown; review 0/1 knapsack and its hard variants (large W -> dp over value; extra dimensions; meet-in-the-middle).
solution:
1. Statement too vague to solve the actual problem.
2. Base: dp[w] descending loop.
3. If W is huge (1e9) but values small: dp[v] = min weight to reach value v; answer max v with dp[v] <= W.
4. If n <= 40 and W huge: meet in the middle (split halves, sort sums, binary search).
5. Extra constraints add dimensions (count, groups, adjacency).
dry_run:
Own example (dp over value): items (w,v)=(3,30),(4,50),(5,60), W=8.
min weight: value 80 -> 7 (3+4), value 90 -> 8 (3+5), value 110 -> 9 (4+5) > 8.
Answer 90.

brief: Items with sizes A[1..N] are processed in order into a bag of size S (each item must fit, wasting S - size); the bag size may be changed at most K times. Minimise total wasted space (LC 1959).
key_idea: K changes = at most K+1 segments; a segment [j..i] costs max*len - sum; dp[i][k] = min over last segment start.
solution:
1. dp[i][k] = min waste for the first i items using k resizes (k+1 segments); dp[0][*]=0.
2. For each end i, walk j from i down to 1 keeping running max and sum: cost = mx*(i-j+1) - sum.
3. dp[i][k] = min(dp[j-1][k-1] + cost) for k>=1; k=0 means one segment from item 1.
4. Answer min over k<=K of dp[N][k] (monotone, so dp[N][K]).
5. Edge cases: K>=N-1 -> 0.
complexity: O(N^2 * K) time (6.4e7 at limits), O(N*K) space

brief: Find the longest non-decreasing subsequence in which every two consecutive chosen elements differ by 0 or by a power of 2.
key_idea: best[v] = longest valid subsequence ending with value v so far; x can follow x itself or x - 2^p.
solution:
1. Scan left to right with unordered_map<long long,int> best.
2. For x: cur = 1 + max(best[x], best[x-1], best[x-2], best[x-4], ..., best[x-2^p]) for all 2^p <= x - minValue (about 31-62 lookups).
3. best[x] = max(best[x], cur); ans = max(ans, cur).
4. Non-decreasing means predecessor values are <= x, so only x - 2^p is checked (not x + 2^p).
5. Edge cases: negatives fine (just look up), use long long.
complexity: O(n * 31) expected time with hashing, O(n) space

brief: Split an array into exactly K non-empty contiguous subarrays; a subarray's dominance score is the maximum frequency of any element in it. Maximise the sum of dominance scores.
key_idea: Precompute mode[l][r] for all subarrays in O(n^2), then dp[g][i] = max over j of dp[g-1][j] + mode[j][i-1].
solution:
1. Compress values; for each l extend r, update freq and running max -> mode[l][r].
2. dp[0][0]=0; dp[g][i] = max_{j in [g-1, i-1]} dp[g-1][j] + mode[j][i-1].
3. Answer dp[K][n] (K>n impossible).
4. Complexity O(K n^2); fine for n ~ 500.
5. Edge cases: K=1 -> mode of whole array; K=n -> n.
